summary: Nathan Lambert reflects on the reasoning model landscape six months after RL with verifiable rewards became mainstream. While scaling RL and inference-time scaling are well understood, the key question is what comes beyond high benchmark scores. He proposes a four-trait taxonomy: skills (math and code, largely achieved), calibration (matching token budget to problem difficulty), strategy (choosing the right direction and knowing alternatives), and abstraction (autonomously decomposing problems, managing memory, and orchestrating parallel compute). Planning—comprising strategy and abstraction—is the next frontier. Calibration is an urgent practical gap: reasoning models waste 10–100x tokens on trivial questions, burdening infrastructure and frustrating users. Strategy is illustrated by DeepSeek R1 diving into computation without planning, risking wasted spend against 1–30 minute agent timeouts. Abstraction extends to agent memory management (Claude Code compresses context, but this may not be optimal), problem decomposition, and calling multiple models in parallel rather than requiring users to do so manually. Lambert draws on the Q*-to-strawberry-to-O1 arc, noting OpenAI spent 12–18 months building initial reasoning traces; a similar effort is needed for planning, but he is more optimistic because experts can readily write 5–10 step plans, unlike 10,000-token reasoning traces. The training path: collect initial planning data, SFT, then RL to reinforce planning styles. He distinguishes skill from planning using O3: extremely skilled at niche search, but deep research produces inconsistent masterpiece-or-dud results due to lack of planning. Parallel compute (O1 Pro, O3 Pro) differs from traditional inference scaling—it makes answers more robust rather than enabling 0-to-1 capability. Lambert outlines a research plan at AI2: collect verified-answer questions, filter by difficulty relative to the base model, run stable RL, then apply methods like overlong filtering for marginal gains. He provocatively suggests renaming post-training as training, noting that if O1 used ~1% of compute on post-training and O3 increased that 10x, compute parity between pretraining and post-training is approaching faster than expected. DeepSeek's original paper used 0.18% of compute on post-training, but with R1 training lasting weeks against a two-month pretraining, that could already be 10–20% of total compute.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Reasoning model skills (math, code) are largely achieved; planning (strategy + abstraction) is the next research frontier.
Calibration—matching token spend to difficulty—is urgent; reasoning models waste 10–100x tokens on trivial questions.
Strategy means choosing the right direction and knowing alternatives; current models dive into problems without planning and struggle to restart.
Abstraction covers memory management, problem decomposition, and parallel model orchestration—capabilities models lack natively.
Training planning is more tractable than reasoning: experts can write 5–10 step plans, unlike 10,000-token reasoning traces with backtracking.
O3 is extremely skilled at search but deep research yields inconsistent results (masterpiece or dud) due to lack of planning.
Parallel compute (O1 Pro, O3 Pro) makes answers more robust, distinct from inference-time scaling that enables 0-to-1 capability.
A practical RL research plan: collect verified questions, filter by base-model difficulty, run stable RL; marginal gains come from methods like overlong filtering.
Post-training compute is rapidly approaching parity with pretraining—O1 used ~1%, O3 increased 10x, and DeepSeek may already be at 10–20%.
Continued AI progress requires deliberate human effort and new research, not automatic scaling.

sections.title: The Current State of Reasoning in AI Models
sections.summary: Lambert reflects on the reasoning model landscape six months after RLVR became mainstream. While scaling RL and inference-time scaling are well understood, the key question is where things are heading beyond high benchmark scores with large token budgets.

sections.title: Unlocking New Language Model Applications
sections.summary: Reasoning models are unlocking genuinely new applications: O3 for finding obscure information, deep research, Claude Code, and emerging autonomous agents. These stem from a step-change in reasoning performance.

sections.title: The Need for Advanced Planning in AI
sections.summary: A plot of task time-horizon shows O1 pushing beyond GPT-4o's saturation. Gains require deliberate human effort and new approaches beyond low-level reasoning skills.

sections.title: A Proposed Taxonomy for Next-Generation Reasoning
sections.summary: Lambert introduces four traits: skills (done), calibration (token budget matching), strategy (choosing direction and alternatives), and abstraction (decomposing problems). Strategy and abstraction are the new planning frontier.

sections.title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
sections.summary: Describes RLVR simply: generate completions, score them, update weights. Currently single-turn; multi-turn with tools is more complex but the core idea remains.

sections.title: Skills and Eval Gains from Reasoning Training
sections.summary: Reviews extraordinary eval gains from O1 and O3. Tool use is being added to reasoning models (DeepSeek, Qwen), with O3's combination feeling qualitatively different.

sections.title: Calibration: The Overthinking Problem
sections.summary: Reasoning models waste 10–100x tokens on simple questions, burdening infrastructure and frustrating users who must switch models or providers.

sections.title: Strategy: Planning Before Acting
sections.summary: DeepSeek R1 dives into computation without planning, risking wasted spend and latency timeouts in agent applications expecting 1–30 minute responses.

sections.title: Abstraction: Memory Management and Parallel Compute
sections.summary: Lambert elaborates on abstraction for agent applications: memory management (Claude Code compresses context, but may not be optimal), tractable problem decomposition, offloading challenging parts, and enabling models to call multiple models in parallel rather than requiring users to do so manually.

sections.title: The Effort Required to Build Planning Capabilities
sections.summary: Drawing on the Q*-to-O1 arc, Lambert notes OpenAI spent 12–18 months building initial reasoning traces. A similar effort is needed for planning, but he is more optimistic because experts can readily write 5–10 step plans. The training path: collect initial data, SFT, then RL to reinforce planning styles.

sections.title: Skills vs Planning: The Deep Research Gap
sections.summary: Lambert distinguishes skill from planning using O3: extremely skilled at niche search, but deep research yields inconsistent masterpiece-or-dud results due to lack of planning. As planning improves, coverage and reliability will increase.

sections.title: Parallel Compute and the Four-Trait Summary
sections.summary: Lambert summarizes the taxonomy, noting strategy and abstraction could be combined as context management. He highlights parallel compute (O1 Pro, O3 Pro) as distinct from inference-time scaling: it makes answers more robust rather than enabling 0-to-1 capability. RL encourages exploration; parallel compute exploits and refines.

sections.title: A Research Plan for Training Reasoning Models
sections.summary: Lambert outlines AI2's research plan: (1) collect verified-answer questions across domains (mostly math and code); (2) filter by difficulty relative to the base model, removing 0/100 and 100/100 questions to avoid wasting compute and noising gradients; (3) run stable RL with numbers going up. Core is stable infrastructure and data; methods like overlong filtering provide marginal gains.

sections.title: The Shift Toward Post-Training Compute Parity
sections.summary: Lambert provocatively suggests renaming post-training as training. If O1 used ~1% of compute on post-training and O3 increased that 10x, compute parity is approaching. DeepSeek's original paper used 0.18% post-training compute, but R1 training lasting weeks against two-month pretraining could already be 10–20%. Scaling RL is very real and should be embraced.

demonstrations: Asked O3 to find an obscure RL concept (coastrunners/overoptimization) and it returned the download link directly.
Used Claude Code with a company API key for casual website-building tasks.
Tested DeepSeek R1 0528 on a frontier math problem and observed it diving directly into polynomial construction without upfront planning.
Described O3 as extremely skilled at niche search but inconsistent in deep research (masterpiece or dud).
Referenced O1 Pro as a robust model using parallel compute rather than traditional inference-time scaling.
limitations: Models lack calibration, wasting tokens on easy problems and frustrating users with latency.
Current reasoning models do very little planning natively; they dive into problems without sketching approaches.
Models struggle to change course or restart plans once committed to a direction.
Abstraction—breaking problems into tractable subtasks—is not done natively by current models.
Claude Code's context compression may not be optimal for every agent application.
Deep research produces inconsistent results (masterpiece or dud) due to lack of planning.
Continual learning has a significant algorithmic bottleneck.
Fully autonomous coding agents currently lack GPU access and internet, limiting ML utility.
quantitativeClaims: Reasoning models can use hundreds to a thousand tokens for questions answerable in one token.
Switching to reasoning models can yield a 10–100x increase in token spend.
DeepSeek R1 on frontier math outputs 10–40,000 tokens per query.
Agent applications typically expect latency between 1 and 30 minutes before timeout.
OpenAI spent 12–18 months building initial reasoning traces for O1.
O1 used approximately 1% of compute on post-training relative to pretraining.
O3 increased post-training compute by 10x relative to O1.
DeepSeek's original paper used 0.18% of compute on post-training in GPU hours.
DeepSeek pre-training takes about two months; R1 training took a few weeks.
DeepSeek's R1 training could represent 10–20% of total compute on the same cluster.
